title: New Specialized Tarmac vs Trek Madone vs Pinarello Dogma F: Top 2026 race bikes compared
content:
Cyclist
New Specialized Tarmac vs Trek Madone vs Pinarello Dogma F: Top 2026 race bikes compared

If you’re looking for a top-end road race bike, the Specialized Tarmac, Trek Madone and Pinarello Dogma F are three bikes that have surely made your shortlist. With the Tarmac SL9, Specialized has copied Pinarello in making small, incremental changes to its race bike. In contrast, the eighth generation Trek Madone was a more radical update over the Gen 7 Madone, slimming down the distinctive design, so that the new bike was significantly lighter.

All three bikes are raced at the top level of pro cycling and, at the top of their respective ranges, bear a pricetag to match. But Specialized, Trek and Pinarello also offer more affordable options that share the DNA of their premium models, so you’re not committed to spending £10,000-plus if you are looking for a race bike from any of the three brands.

Specialized applies its S-Works branding to its premium Tarmacs and Pinarello only uses the Dogma tag for its top spec F-series bike, as well as its Dogma X endurance bike and Dogma GR gravel race bike. Trek is more generous with its Madone label, using it for the whole range, but differentiates between the premium SLR and lower carbon grade SL framesets.

We’ll guide you through the three bikes’ key features and the available ranges and, lower down, we’ll make some suggestions for how to choose between them.

New Specialized Tarmac vs Trek Madone vs Pinarello Dogma key features

Specialized Tarmac SL9

  • Lightweight/aero race bike
  • Two carbon grades: FACT 12r (S-Works), FACT 10r
  • S-Level spec with premium components on FACT 10r frameset
  • SL9 upgrades now for both framesets level
  • 32mm tyre clearance

Trek Madone Gen 8

  • Generation 8 is both aero and low in weight
  • Two carbon frame grades: OCLV 900, OCLV 500
  • Trek Race Geometry
  • Aero bar/stem on SLR specs
  • 32mm tyre clearance

Pinarello Dogma F / F-series

  • Dogma F is premium bike with a range of cheaper alternatives
  • Asymmetric aero frame design
  • Four carbon grades: M40X in Dogma F, T900, T700 and T600 in F-Series
  • F9, F7, F5, F3 and F1 bikes with less premium carbon, higher weights and lower specs and prices
  • 32mm tyre clearance

Specialized Tarmac vs Trek Madone vs new Pinarello Dogma F latest updates 

The Madone and the Dogma F were updated more or less at the same time, just ahead of the 2024 Tour de France. The Tarmac was updated in advance of the 2026 Tour, but the SL9 update was initially confined to the premium FACT 12 S-Works frameset, before being extended to non-S-Works bikes built on the FACT 10 frame in August 2026.

The Madone had the most radical makeover of the three bikes, with the Gen 8 bike essentially a significantly slimmed-down version of the Gen 7 bike. It retains the dramatic IsoFlow seat tube design with the central hole under the seatpost, but pares everything down to lose around 300g in mass.  

In contrast, the Dogma F’s weight-shedding hacks have been more modest, although it too has been on a diet, losing a claimed 108g. It now incorporates a narrower, longer head tube, narrower down tube and new, shorter thru-axles, which are enveloped by the frame at their far ends. The lower spec F-series bikes were last updated in 2025 and now have much in common with the Dogma F.

The Tarmac was the most recent of the three bikes to be updated, the S-Works in June and the non-S-Works in August 2026, and it also saw modest changes. The SL9’s frontal area has been reduced and the fork legs deepened, while the seat tube now merges more smoothly with the seat stays. Together, Specialized claims the updates save 4 watts at 45km/h.

Specialized Tarmac vs Trek Madone vs Pinarello Dogma F aerodynamics

The Tarmac SL9 retains the SL8’s ‘Speed Sniffer’ head tube bulge, but it’s less prominent, due to the deeper head tube shape. Specialized has narrowed the head tube though, reducing the SL9’s frontal area by 10% relative to the SL8. That’s necessitated the rerouting of the brake hoses, so that they both pass to one side of the fork steerer.

In turn, Specialized has had to design a steerer tube with an asymmetric kink in it. It still works with the same Roval one-piece cockpits and separate Roval bars and stem as the SL8 though.

The new seat tube design includes what Specialized calls a ‘Win Fin’ that fills the gap between the seat tube and seat stays, which it says improves airflow, while additional aero improvements come from a 2mm deeper seat tube and a narrower seatpost.

Despite the shallower tube profiles and smaller IsoFlow cavity under the seatpost, Trek says that the Gen 8 Madone is as aero as the Gen 7 bike, in art thanks to the adoption of new aero bottles and cages. The bar-stem on the SLR bikes is thicker than the Gen 7’s, which Trek says improves airflow further back, directing it away from the rider’s legs.

The loosening of the UCI’s frame geometry rules has allowed Pinarello to deepen the head tube in the latest generation Dogma F, with a pronounced ‘nose’ to help aerodynamics, as with the Tarmac. The new bike also has a ‘keel’ under the bottom bracket, which Pinarello says helps airflow, while the seat tube and seatpost are thinned down.

The 2025 F-Series bikes follow the same design principles as the Dogma F, although tube profiles have less sharp trailing edges, suiting the less exotic carbon fibre that is used. The Dogma F’s keel is now a feature and the frame of the F9 and F7 is compatible with the same Talon Ultra Fast cockpit as the Dogma F.

Specialized Tarmac vs Trek Madone vs Pinarello Dogma F weight

Previous generations of the Dogma F bikes, stretching back to the F8, used to be on the heavy side for pro-level race bikes, which is why Ineos Grenadiers persisted in riding the Dogma F12 with rim brakes after other pro teams had made the switch to disc brakes. The latest Dogma F has shed enough weight to better the UCI’s 6.8kg weight limit, even with disc brakes – the only choice, as Pinarello no longer offers a rim brake option. We weighed our size 56 review bike at 6.7kg.

Likewise, the Madone Gen 7 was chunky enough that pro riders took to the Emonda for mountain stages. That’s changed with the Gen 8 Madone, which now has a 7kg claimed weight in premium specs, leading to the demise of the Emonda. We weighed our size L review bike at 7.4kg, but that included Trek’s aero bottles and cages.

The Specialized S-Works Tarmac SL9 too is right on the 6.8kg UCI weight limit for the top spec bikes, as was the SL8, with Specialized claiming that frame weight is near-identical, despite the extra material in the SL9 frame. We weighed a size 58 at 7kg, again with bottle cages attached. 

As you’d expect, when you drop down the range for all three brands weights increase, driven by less expensive, heavier carbon layups and the selection of lower priced components. 

Specialized Tarmac vs Trek Madone vs Pinarello Dogma F sizing

Trek has narrowed down the range of sizes offered for the Madone from eight for the Gen 7 bike to six for the Gen 8. It says that this has reduced overlaps between frame sizes, so that choosing the right frame size is easier for riders who fall on the boundary between two sizes. At the same time, riders at the short and tall end of the height spectrum are better accommodated, with sizes claimed to fit rider heights between 143cm and 213cm.

In contrast, Pinarello sells the Dogma F in 11 sizes and the F-series frame in nine sizes, which it says is more than any of its competitors, helping buyers to choose the right fit for them. It recommends you visit a dealer to help choose the correct size frame for you.

The Tarmac SL9 is sold in seven sizes, offering slightly greater frame size choice than the Madone but still not as much as Pinarello. It is claimed to cater for riders from 142cm to 196cm tall.

Specialized Tarmac vs Trek Madone vs Pinarello Dogma F handlebars

With the top spec bikes including an integrated bar/stem, choosing the right combination for you is important. Trek has 21 different bar width/stem length combinations from 380x80mm up to 440x120mm, with the Aero RSL bar/stem on the SLR bikes being 30mm narrower on the tops than in the drops.

The Dogma F’s Most Talon Ultra Fast bar/stem also has a flared profile and is available in 28 different width/length combinations. Pinarello measures its bar widths from the outside of the drops, so its available 400mm to 460mm widths are actually 20mm narrower than they appear and in line with the Madone.

The Tarmac’s Roval Rapide Cockpit comes in 15 sizes, covering the same 380mm to 420mm range. It’s not as flared as the Trek and Pinarello bars at just 4 degrees, giving you more hand space on the tops, but potentially a slightly less aero ride position on the hoods.

While the higher spec bikes use a one-piece design, in all three ranges lower spec bikes revert to a separate bar and stem which together offer greater adjustability.

Geometry-wise the three bikes have a lot in common, as indicated by the comparison above of their size 56-equivalent frames. The Tarmac is a little longer than the other two bikes, as shown by the frame reach and wheelbase, while Pinarello’s head tube length is shorter and its angle slacker than the Madone or Tarmac. Despite this, its stack is near-identical. Pinarello doesn’t offer offset or trail figures, so we can’t judge whether these compensate for the slacker head tube.

Pinarello’s geometry is the same between the Dogma F and other F-Series bikes, although there’s an additional size 600 available for the Dogma F. Although it’s not the only brand to build its bikes asymmetrically, the brand emphasises its asymmetric design, particularly in the rear triangle, which it claims helps even out forces acting on the frame due to the drivetrain.

The trend across performance bike makers is to slim down the seat tube. That makes placement of the internal battery for Shimano electronic groupsets more difficult; whereas previous generations of the bikes had the battery housed in the seatpost, that’s no longer possible.

Pinarello houses its Di2 battery under a weatherproof cover in the bottom of the seat tube. The Madone Gen 8’s Di2 battery also resides in the bottom of the seat tube in a separate housing and is inserted through the bottom bracket, while Specialized uses a sleeve that holds the battery below the seatpost.

Specialized Tarmac vs Trek Madone vs Pinarello Dogma F groupset options

The premium specs all get a choice of top-of-the-range groupsets, either Shimano Dura-Ace or SRAM Red. Pinarello has in the past also offered a Campagnolo Super Record option. The Trek Madone is also available as a 1x spec, fitted with 12-speed SRAM Rex AXS.

As usual, move down the price scale and you’ll move down the groupset spec. Trek finishes with a mechanical Shimano 105 base spec, while Pinarello stops at the electronic 105 Di2 and Specialized at SRAM Rival.

A power meter is increasingly seen as an essential for a performance-oriented bike and offered factory-fitted to many higher spec bikes from multiple brands. Here, Specialized does best, with both Shimano and SRAM specs including a power meter.

Trek is more frugal, not fitting a power meter to its Shimano specs, but speccing the in-series power meters to its SRAM bikes. In contrast, Pinarello does not offer specs with a power meter for any of its bikes.

Specialized Tarmac vs Trek Madone vs Pinarello Dogma F wheels

All three brands offer premium wheels on their top spec bikes. In the case of the Madone, these come from Trek’s in-house Bontrager Aeolus range, while Specialized fits its Roval Rapide CLX III wheels.

Pinarello offers the wavy rimmed Princeton Carbonworks Peak 4550 DB wheels on both its Shimano and SRAM spec Dogma bikes.

Lower down the bike ranges, all three brands offer lower spec in-house carbon wheels, while Trek and Pinarello’s lowest spec bikes are in each case equipped with alloy rim wheels. All the bikes can be set up tubeless.

Specialized Tarmac vs Trek Madone vs Pinarello Dogma F tyre clearance

All three bikes offer moderately large tyre clearance, which is up on previous generations of their framesets. For a race-oriented bike, tyre clearance, particularly in the rear triangle, is a balancing act: more clearance in general means longer chainstays, which lead to less snappy performance, which potentially downgrades the racy ride feel.

Both Trek and Specialized have increased their clearance to allow 32mm tyres, while Pinarello has stayed at 30mm for the Dogma F, but increased to 32mm for the F Series frames.

Specialized Tarmac vs Trek Madone vs Pinarello F frame grades

The Pinarello Dogma F makes use of a new carbon fibre recently introduced by Toray. Called M40X, it’s claimed to provide a high-tensile modulus, which Pinarello says allowed it to reduce weight but still make the frameset even stiffer than its predecessor.

Both Trek and Specialized also claim lighter and stiffer properties for their latest carbon fibre mixes in their top spec bikes. They’re likely to be similar to Pinarello’s, as there are limited sources for premium carbon fibre, although they have proprietary names: OCLV 900 and FACT 12r, respectively.

All three brands use lower spec carbon that’s less expensive but heavier further down their ranges. Trek calls its version OCLV 500, while Specialized has FACT 10r. Pinarello uses Toray T900 fibre in its F9 and F7, T700 fibre in its F5 and F3 framesets and T600 in the F1.

Specialized Tarmac vs Trek Madone vs Pinarello Dogma F: Which should you choose?

If you’re in the market for a premium spec bike, you’re spoiled for choice. All three brands offer pro-level options equipped with drivetrains from SRAM and Shimano. They all fit wheels and other components to match and prices are comparable between brands.

All three claim class-leading aerodynamics and UCI-skimming weights too. Absent any direct comparisons to back that up, choice is to a large extent a matter of personal preference – and looks. The inclusion or absence of a power meter might be a deciding factor though, particularly for Shimano spec bikes.

Pinarello Dogma bikes have always been an aspirational purchase and the distinctive frame design turns heads even among non-cyclists, although it remains divisive.

In contrast, the Tarmac SL9, notwithstanding its racing palmares, looks more like a classic race bike and blends into the crowd more.

That’s not true of the Madone, which like the Pinarello F is a head-turner. 

If you’re looking further down the price range, all three brands cater for the mid-level purchase, although you’ll get better value from the American brands. Only Trek and Pinarello offer a more affordable base spec with mechanical 105.
